headline: Projection Bias: when today's state writes tomorrow's contract
lede: Projection bias is the tendency to assume that our future selves will want roughly what we want right now. It matters most when a temporary state — hunger, enthusiasm, exhaustion, a cold week — quietly shapes a commitment whose costs will arrive later, in a different state.

sections.heading: What the pattern is and where it appears
paragraphs: Most people know, in the abstract, that their tastes change. Projection bias is not ignorance of that fact; it is underestimating how much the change will be. The person signing a two-year gym contract in a burst of January motivation does not believe motivation is eternal. They simply price the contract as if January motivation were close to the long-run average. The bias lives in the gap between 'I know I will change' and the much smaller change actually imagined.

The decisions most exposed to this pattern share a structure: they are made in one state and paid for in another. Long-term purchases, career commitments, dietary plans made right after lunch, subscriptions bought during a free trial week, leases signed while a city still feels novel. In each case the current state feels like evidence about the future, even when it is really just weather — literal or emotional — passing through.

sections.heading: Why the current state wins the forecast
paragraphs: The mechanism, as the reviewed evidence describes it, is incomplete adjustment. Today's tastes, hunger, mood or circumstances provide a salient starting point for any prediction about the future. We adjust away from that anchor — we are not naive — but the adjustment tends to be too small. The present is vivid and free; the future self is an abstraction. Vivid beats abstract in most forecasting contests.

This is not purely a laboratory finding. Field evidence on catalog orders found that weather conditions on the day of an order influenced decisions whose consequences arrived much later, even though those conditions were never going to persist. An unusually cold day nudged people toward cold-weather purchases they later returned at higher rates. The shoppers were not irrational in a general sense; they were letting a transient state do work it had no business doing.

sections.heading: What the evidence supports, and what it does not
paragraphs: The evidence base is strongest in intertemporal choice and consumer settings: predicting what you will want to eat later, what you will use later, what you will enjoy later. There, the pattern of overprojecting current states onto future preferences is reasonably well established, through theory, incentivized experiments and field data. That is a solid but bounded foundation.

What the evidence does not support is using projection bias as a generic explanation for every wrong prediction anyone makes about their future self. A bad forecast can come from missing information, changing circumstances, or plain randomness, none of which is this bias. The reviewed evidence also does not license claims that people never learn, that preferences are arbitrary, or that every long commitment is a mistake. Sometimes the gym membership works out. The bias claim is narrower: current states systematically get too much weight in the forecast.

sections.heading: Do not confuse it with the hot-cold empathy gap
paragraphs: Projection bias is often mixed up with the hot-cold empathy gap, and the two are close relatives. The empathy gap concerns failing to appreciate how a different visceral state — pain, craving, fear, arousal — changes motivation and choice, either in your future self or in other people. Projection bias is the broader forecasting error of carrying today's tastes and states into tomorrow's preferences with too little correction.

The distinction matters because the checks differ slightly. For an empathy gap, the key question is whether a specific visceral state is doing the distorting: 'Am I calm now, predicting a decision I will make while tempted?' For projection bias, the question is wider: 'Which part of my current situation — mood, novelty, appetite, fatigue — am I quietly assuming will still be true in a year?' A related concept, impact bias, concerns overestimating how intense or long-lasting future emotions will be; that is about feelings after an event, not about preferences across time.

sections.heading: A compact example: the equipment bought in the wrong season
paragraphs: Consider someone who, during an unusually harsh week in November, orders an expensive set of winter gear — premium jacket, heavy boots, the works. The purchase total is around a month's discretionary budget. By February the winter has been ordinary, the gear has been worn twice, and by spring it is competing for closet space with last year's optimism. Nothing about the shopper was foolish. The forecast was contaminated by the week it was made in.

A better procedure does not require ignoring the cold week; it may genuinely signal a need. It requires a second measurement. Wait until a normal week and re-ask the question. Check the reference class: how often did last year's winters actually demand this gear, and what happened to previous seasonal purchases? If the need survives a neutral state and a look at history, buy. If it only exists during the cold snap, the state was making the decision, not the person.

checklist: Before a long commitment, write down the current state you are in: mood, energy, hunger, novelty, season.
Re-evaluate the same decision in a meaningfully different state — rested versus exhausted, busy versus calm — before signing.
Ask how your preferences on this topic have actually changed over the past five years, and use that as a reference class.
For purchases, check how often the relevant condition (weather, workload, motivation) has occurred in the past year rather than this week.
Add a waiting period to expensive or hard-to-reverse decisions made during an unusual state.
Prefer contracts and plans with exit options when your forecast depends on your current enthusiasm lasting.
After a commitment fails, check whether the error was state contamination or missing information before drawing a lesson.
boundaryNote: Projection bias helps you inspect whether a temporary state is inflating a forecast of future preferences; it does not prove that any particular long-term commitment is wrong, that preferences are unstable, or that a failed prediction was caused by this bias rather than by new information or chance.
